925.title: Duties of the Heart
925.hook: Bahya ibn Paquda teaches that outward practice needs inner work
925.howItsDone: Duties of the Heart is studied in Jewish ethical and spiritual learning, especially in the Musar tradition, and its gate on trust in God is read on its own by some as a guide to bitachon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kuzari. Your line was the king asks. Today, the king's problem turned inside out.

A to-do list on the fridge: groceries, call the dentist, return the library book. By evening, every item is checked off. But nothing on it says be patient with the kids, or stop resenting your brother, or trust that tomorrow will hold. Those don't fit in a box. Yesterday's king had the right intentions and the wrong actions. Today's teacher saw the opposite risk: you can do every right action and leave the heart behind. His name was Bahya ibn Paquda, a judge in Muslim Spain, and his book is called Duties of the Heart.
screen: `A LIST OF THINGS TO CHECK OFF.` → `WHAT DOESN'T FIT IN A BOX.` → `BAHYA'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: Bahya divides the commandments into two kinds. Duties of the limbs, things you do with your body: keep the Sabbath, give charity, pray aloud, eat this and not that. And duties of the heart, things that happen inside: believing God is one, trusting God, loving God, being humble, being sorry for wrong, examining yourself honestly. In his introduction he says he found long, careful books on the outward duties and very little on the inner ones, so he wrote this one to fill the gap. One proof text comes from the Shema. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Love can't be done with your hands; it's a duty of the heart. The same idea sounds in the story of David's anointing, where the prophet is told: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Bahya arranges the book in gates, one for each inner duty, including a whole gate on trust. He isn't against outward practice; the limbs and the heart need each other. In a picture: commandments with no heart are like a lamp with no oil, and good intentions with no deeds are just as incomplete. In one story, a pious man meets soldiers coming home from battle with their spoils. He tells them they've come back from the lesser war, and must now prepare for the greater one, inside: the struggle with your own inclinations. No army can fight that one for you.
screen: `DUTIES OF THE LIMBS.` · `DUTIES OF THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.` · `THE LESSER WAR AND THE GREATER WAR.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing from Bahya's list that nobody can see you do: hand one worry over for these breaths, be glad of someone who did better than you, or look honestly at one moment from yesterday. Notice how it feels to leave no mark on any list. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer in your own words.

926.title: Abraham ibn Ezra
926.hook: traveler, poet, grammarian and sharp-eyed commentator
926.howItsDone: Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary is printed alongside the Torah in editions of the Mikraot Gedolot, the rabbinic Bible, and students read him for his attention to grammar and plain meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bahya's Duties of the Heart. Your line was the greater war is inside. Today, a man who couldn't stay put.

If I sold candles, the sun would never set. That's the gist of a short Hebrew poem, a joke a poet made about his own luck. If he dealt in burial shrouds, he goes on, nobody would die as long as he lived. Whatever he tried, the world arranged itself so that he couldn't make a living. The man who wrote that was not a failure. He was a sharp-eyed reader of the Bible, a grammarian, an astronomer, a poet, and a wanderer who carried his books from city to city. Today, Abraham ibn Ezra.
screen: `CANDLES, AND THE SUN NEVER SETS.` → `A POET LAUGHS AT HIS LUCK.` → `A WANDERER WITH BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ezra grew up in Muslim Spain, in the world of the poets we've met this week. Then he left, and kept moving: Italy, France and, by his own writings, as far as England. Wherever he stayed, he wrote. Spanish Jewish learning had grown up in Arabic, and Arabic was not the language of the Jews of Christian Europe. So ibn Ezra did something simple and huge: he wrote it out in Hebrew. Grammar books, astronomy, and above all commentaries on the Bible. As a commentator he wanted the plain meaning of the words, what Hebrew calls peshat. He paid close attention to grammar: how a verb is built, why a word is spelled the way it is. He could be blunt with interpretations he thought ignored the words on the page. And he had a sharp eye for the odd detail. When Abram first arrives in the land, Genesis says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And the Canaanite was then in the land." Then? Ibn Ezra noticed that little word. He wrote that there is a secret here, and that the one who understands it should keep silent. He doesn't say what the secret is. Readers have argued ever since: some read it as a hint about who wrote that line and when; others read it differently. That's very ibn Ezra: sharp, brief, and willing to leave a question hanging. A traveler learns to notice what locals stop seeing. Maybe that's why he saw so much in a word like then. He left behind commentaries that Jews still print beside the Torah.
screen: `A WANDERER: ITALY, FRANCE, ENGLAND.` · `SPANISH LEARNING CARRIED INTO HEBREW.` · `PESHAT: THE PLAIN MEANING.` · then, large: `AND THE CANAANITE WAS THEN IN THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Say the verse once, slowly: and the Canaanite was then in the land. Now read it the way ibn Ezra did: which word stops you, and what question would you write in the margin? You don't need an answer; if you pray, you can ask in your own words to read with open eyes.

927.title: Maimonides' life
927.hook: born in Córdoba, he fled persecution and became a physician in Cairo
927.howItsDone: Jews around the world study the Rambam's Mishneh Torah, some following a daily study cycle, and his Thirteen Principles appear in prayer books in the form of the hymn Yigdal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ibn Ezra, who never stayed long in one city. Your line was the traveler. Today, another traveler, though not by choice.

A student wanted to visit a busy man in Egypt, and the man wrote back a warning: come if you like, but don't expect a long talk. Each morning he went to the palace as a doctor. When he rode home, his hallway was already full: Jews and non-Jews, officials and ordinary people, all waiting to see him. He took one quick meal, then treated them until night. That picture comes from the letter itself. The same man wrote a law code people still study and a philosophy book people still argue about. And he started out in Spain, in Córdoba, with a long road of flight between the two. Today, the life of the Rambam.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CROWDED HALLWAY.` → `A LETTER TO A STUDENT.` → `CÓRDOBA TO CAIRO.`

segments.voice: Rambam is a name built from initials: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon. English speakers often call him Maimonides, son of Maimon. His father was a judge and scholar in Córdoba, and the boy grew up in that learned city. Then the ground shifted. A new ruling movement, the Almohads, took power in Muslim Spain and North Africa and pressed Jews and Christians to convert or leave. The family chose the road: from place to place in Spain, across to Fez in Morocco, east to the land of Israel, and finally to Fustat, the old city of Cairo. Picture it for a young scholar: books carried in bags, teachers left behind, no settled home for years. And yet he kept writing the whole way, a commentary on the Mishnah begun on the move. In Egypt he became a physician, and in time a doctor to the court. He led the Jewish community, answered legal questions in letters, and finished his great code of law, the Mishneh Torah, and later his philosophy book, the Guide for the Perplexed. The Torah keeps reminding a people who had been strangers how to treat strangers. In the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Rambam had been a stranger in many lands. He ended up in Egypt itself, and his door was open to whoever came.

928.title: The letter to Yemen
928.hook: Maimonides writes to encourage persecuted Jews in Yemen
928.howItsDone: The letter to Yemen is studied today as an example of Jewish leadership in hard times, and Yemenite Jews have long honored the Rambam's writings and memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rambam's road from Córdoba to Cairo. Your line was from córdoba to cairo. Today, a letter he sent south.

The news from the far south of Arabia is bad. It reaches Egypt in a letter from Jacob, a leader of the Jews of Yemen. A new ruler there is pressing Jews to convert, and some have given in. A preacher who converted is telling people their own scriptures point to his faith. And in one town a man claims to be the messiah, and people are following him. Jacob asks a stranger far away what to tell his frightened community. The man he wrote to had once been a refugee from that very kind of pressure. Today, the letter that came back.
screen: `BAD NEWS FROM YEMEN.` → `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` → `A QUESTION SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The answer is known in Hebrew as Iggeret Teiman, the letter to Yemen. The Rambam wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of his readers, so ordinary people could follow it. And it is warm. He opens with praise for Jacob and the community, and he doesn't scold the ones who are wavering. Then he takes their three troubles in turn. The pressure: hard times have come before, he says, and the people outlasted them; hold on to the covenant and don't lose heart. The doubt: to the claim that their own books point somewhere else, he answers that the verses are being bent out of their meaning, and urges them to keep studying their own texts. The false messiah: gently but firmly, he says this man is not who he says he is, and following him puts the whole community in danger. He judges that the man seems unwell in his mind, and advises the community to deal with him quietly, for its own safety. Near the end, something practical: copy this letter and read it aloud in every community, so no one is left alone with the bad news. Its courage runs back to the Torah. As Moses tells the people in the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Be strong and of good courage." Tradition says the Jews of Yemen held this letter dear, and remembered its writer in their prayers. A frightened community wrote to a stranger, and the stranger wrote back as a friend.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ARABIC, FOR EVERYONE.` · `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` · `READ IT ALOUD IN EVERY COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `BE STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Think of one person carrying something hard right now, an illness, a job loss, a lonely stretch, and start a note to them in your head the way the Rambam did: with something true and good about them. Then one plain line of support, and no advice unless they asked. If you pray, you can hold them in your own words first.

929.title: His brother David
929.hook: his brother drowned at sea on a trading voyage; Maimonides grieved for years
929.howItsDone: Jewish mourning moves in stages, with shiva in the first week, shloshim through the first month, a year of saying Kaddish for a parent, and a yahrzeit candle lit on each anniversary of the death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Yemen. Your line was write to encourage. Today, a letter of a different kind, about the Rambam's own loss.

Two brothers, one house. The older one, Moses, sits with his books. The younger one, David, packs for a long trip. He is a merchant, and the family lives on what he earns; that's what lets his brother study and write without worrying about bread. David sets out by sea, heading for India, carrying his own money and money that others have trusted him with. And then the ship goes down. Today, the brother of the Rambam, and what the Rambam himself wrote about his grief.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, ONE HOUSE.` → `A MERCHANT SAILS FOR INDIA.` → `THE SHIP GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: We know this mostly from the Rambam's own words. Years later he wrote to an old friend, a judge in the land of Israel who had once traveled with him. The friend had complained that the Rambam hadn't written in a long time. The answer is deeply personal. The worst thing that ever happened to him, he explains, was the death of his brother, who drowned in the Indian Ocean. For about a year afterward he lay ill, in grief, close to despair. David had been raised on his knees; they had studied together; David had carried the family's business so that he could stay at his desk. David left a young widow and a little daughter, and the Rambam took them in. Then comes the line that gives today its name. Even now, after all this time, he writes, he is still mourning. When he sees David's handwriting or one of his books, the grief comes back. Notice who is saying this: the writer of a vast code of law and a demanding book of philosophy, a man who wrote about the mind and its control of feeling. And he doesn't pretend. He tells his friend plainly that the loss still lives in him. Jewish mourning has its own rhythm: the first week, the first month, the first year, and the yearly day of remembrance after that. The rhythm doesn't say grief ends. It gives grief a shape to walk through, and the Rambam's letter shows a scholar walking through it slowly, and saying so.
screen: `A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.` · `DROWNED IN THE INDIAN OCEAN.` · `HE STILL MOURNED, YEARS LATER.` · then, large: `GRIEF GIVEN A SHAPE.`

If grief comes, let it sit beside you; it doesn't need fixing, and if they're living, think of one thing you'd like them to know. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words.

930.title: Nachmanides
930.hook: a Catalan rabbi who defended Judaism at the Barcelona disputation, then settled in the land of Israel
930.howItsDone: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in study editions of the Bible alongside Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and a synagogue in Jerusalem's Old City bears his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David, the Rambam's brother, still mourned years later. Your line was grief takes years. Today, a name one letter apart.

Rambam, yesterday. Ramban, today. One letter changes, and it's a different man, born about two generations later, in a different country. Moshe ben Maimon became the Rambam. Moshe ben Nachman became the Ramban, and in English, Nachmanides. He lived in Girona, in Catalonia, a doctor and a rabbi, and he wrote a commentary on the Torah that is still printed in study editions today. Then a summons came. The king of Aragon wanted him in Barcelona, in the royal palace, to answer questions about his faith in public, against a man who had been born Jewish and become a Christian friar. He could not refuse.
screen: `RAMBAM, RAMBAN: ONE LETTER APART.` → `A RABBI IN GIRONA.` → `A SUMMONS TO BARCELONA.`

segments.voice: The debate is called the Barcelona disputation. The friar, Pablo Christiani, argued that passages in the rabbis' own writings showed the messiah had already come. The Ramban was asked to respond, in front of the king and church leaders. Picture the risk: a rabbi speaking freely about another faith, before the powerful, could put his whole community in danger. So before he began, by his own account, he asked the king for one thing: permission to speak freely. The king granted it. What we know comes mostly from the Ramban's own written report. There's also a short Latin record from the other side, and the two don't tell it the same way; each side wrote down its own version. What stands out in the Ramban's account is his manner. He answers point by point, from the texts. He says the stories in the Talmud and the midrash are not all binding in the same way as law. He is direct, at times sharp, and respectful of the king, who, he writes, sent him home with a gift. Afterward his account was published, and he faced trouble for it. In time he left Catalonia and made the journey to the land of Israel. In a letter home to his son, he describes Jerusalem as poor and desolate, and tells how he helped gather a few people and set up a place to pray. Strength of argument, without contempt. And when the pressure grew, a new beginning far away.
screen: `ASKED TO ANSWER IN PUBLIC.` · then, large: `PERMISSION TO SPEAK FREELY.` · `POINT BY POINT, FROM THE TEXTS.` · `A NEW START IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Think of one conversation coming up where you'll need to hold your ground, at work, at home, online, and before the words, find the manner. What's the one thing you want to say clearly, and the one thing you won't say, because it would only wound? If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a steady voice.

931.title: The Zohar
931.hook: in Castile, Moses de León circulates the Zohar, the book of radiance
931.howItsDone: Some Jews study the Zohar in groups or read a portion daily, and its teachings shaped customs like the Friday night Kabbalat Shabbat service and some Sabbath songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramban at Barcelona, then a new start in Jerusalem. Your line was defend with dignity. Today, a book wrapped in light.

In a town in Castile, a scholar named Moses de León starts sending out pages: copies, he says, of an old book. It's written mostly in Aramaic, a language of the Talmud, and it reads like a long walk through the Torah with a circle of ancient teachers, led by a rabbi of the Mishnah, Shimon bar Yochai. They stop on a verse, one of them opens it, and the verse turns out to have rooms inside rooms. Scholars, students and mystics begin copying the pages. The book has a one-word name: Zohar.
screen: `PAGES SENT OUT FROM CASTILE.` → `ARAMAIC, LIKE THE TALMUD.` → `A VERSE WITH ROOMS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The name comes from a verse in the book of Daniel. In the JPS translation: "And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament." Brightness there is zohar. So the title means radiance, splendor, a light that shines, and the book is about hidden light. The Zohar reads the Torah as having a surface and a depth: the stories and laws are the garment; underneath is a soul. It speaks of the sefirot, ways that the hidden God is revealed in the world, and it imagines human actions, a prayer, a kind deed, a Sabbath meal, echoing up through those worlds. Now the honest part: who wrote it? There are two answers, both held sincerely. Traditional readers receive the Zohar as the teaching of Shimon bar Yochai and his companions, handed down and later brought to light. Other readers, historians among them, look at its language and its world and conclude it was composed in Castile in the time of Moses de León, by him or a circle around him. There's even an old account of a traveler, Isaac of Acre, who went looking for the ancient original and heard conflicting answers. Both views agree on what happened next. The Zohar became a central book of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical teaching. Its ideas flowed into prayer books, Sabbath songs and later movements of the spirit. People still sit with it slowly, a line at a time, the way its own teachers sit with a verse.
screen: `ZOHAR: BRIGHTNESS, FROM DANIEL.` · then, large: `SHALL SHINE AS THE BRIGHTNESS OF THE FIRMAMENT.` · `A GARMENT AND A SOUL.` · `WHO WROTE IT? TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Take the verse the book is named for, and they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, breathing in on the first half and out on the second. Then ask the Zohar's kind of question, what makes a person shine, and let the line sit without solving it. If you pray, you can carry the verse into your own prayer.
Zohar. Brightness, radiance, from a verse in Daniel: the name of a central book of Jewish mysticism, written mostly in Aramaic and circulated from Castile. Today's word.
Your line: the book of radiance. From the heart's inner war to hidden light: a full week. That's day nine hundred thirty-one.
